newsitem.title: CHINA: Business as usual as HK stock exchange reopens.
newsitem.headline: Business as usual as HK stock exchange reopens.

text.p: There was no champagne, just business as usual when the Hong Kong stock exchange reopened on Thursday after its three-day China handover break.
You had to strain hard to detect a switch from colonial-style trading to Beijing-style capitalism.

A lone small Chinese flag on one trader's work station -- and a complete absence of Britain's Union Jack -- were the only tipoffs that things were not as they were last Friday when the exchange was last open.
There was no speech, no ceremony, no cheer, just the routine opening bell when the clock ticked to 10 a.m. to announce that Hong Kong's favourite pastime, making and losing money, could begin.
As the hour approached, traders delayed by the torrential rainstorms sweeping the territory sprinted to their desks.

Donning the exchange's red vest with gold numbers on it to identify themselves, the stroke of 10 o'clock found nearly all traders either on the phone or with their heads glued to small screens on their desks.
They seemed oblivious to the dozens of journalists and photographers gathered on the floor to record the start of the exchange's new era.
"Everybody is doing their own job and everything is just the same," one trader said.

With financiers around the world watching closely to see how Hong Kong would fare under China's "one country, two systems" formula for reunification, the exchange in the first hours sent its usual mixed messages.
The Hang Seng Index, which had closed at a record high last week as the curtain fell on British rule, leaped by more than one percent to 15,363.61 points at the start of trading.

But then it succumbed to profit-taking and dipped back down again amid fears over government plans to increase housing supply in one of the world's most overcrowded cities. Property stocks led the market down.
"Handover fever is coming to an end and investors are taking a break in the short run before taking new positions," said Edwin Cheung, a senior sales manager at Taiwan Securities.

Hong Kong's economy has risen by almost six percent a year over the past decade and nearly all economists expect the rise to continue, with the switch to Chinese rule not, in the words of the trade, "a market factor".
"No one has ever bet against Hong Kong in the past and won," Hong Kong's Beijing-appointed leader Tung Chee-hwa told top businessmen on the eve of the exchange reopening.
